title: First-Time Hyperglycemia
description: A patient presents with signs of new‑onset hyperglycemia. Learners assess symptoms, perform and interpret bedside glucose results, initiate safety measures, and provide introductory diabetes education.
learningObjective:
Perform a focused assessment of an adult with polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. 
​Perform and interpret bedside glucose and prepare to communicate abnormal findings to the provider using SBAR format. 
Initiate appropriate nursing interventions while ensuring patient safety. 
Provide patient-centered education at an introductory level.

actions.title: Perform Point-of-Care Glucose Test
actions.prompt: Indicate the step-by-step process to follow to safely and effectively perform a point-of-care glucose test in accordance with best-practice guidelines.
items: Power on the glucometer, check the expiration date and integrity of test strips, and insert a new test strip into the meter.
Select a lateral side of a fingertip, place the hand in a dependent position, clean the selected fingertip area with an alcohol wipe, and allow the selected fingertip area to dry completely.
Position the lancet within the cleaned fingertip area, activate the lancet to puncture the skin, dispose of used lancet immediately in sharps container.

Wipe away first drop of blood, gently squeeze finger proximal to puncture site to produce drop of blood, bring test strip in meter to the blood drop, allow capillary action to wick blood into test strip.
Apply clean gauze to puncture site with slight pressure to stop bleeding, then apply bandage to site as needed, and read glucometer results when displayed on meter and verbally share results.
actions.resultName:
Point of Care Glucose: 312 mg/dL 
Normal Range: ~70–110 mg/dL (fasting), up to ~140 mg/dL post prandial 
Interpretation: Marked hyperglycemia; consistent with diabetes and risk of DKA

actions.title: Perform Urine Dipstick Test
actions.prompt: Indicate the step-by-step process to follow to safely and effectively perform a urine dipstick test in accordance with best-practice guidelines.
items: Obtain recently collected urine sample and verify urine sample is labelled correctly and matches patient identity, then check the expiration date and integrity of the urine dipstick test container/supplies and remove only one dipstick without touching the reagent pads

Gently swirl the urine container to resuspend any settled elements and then dip the reagent end of the test strip fully into the urine, ensure all pads are briefly but completely immersed, then remove the test strip and run the edge of the edge of the strip along the rim of the container to remove excess urine while keeping the strip horizontal

Keeping the strip horizontal, place the strip flat on a clean, absorbent surface with pads facing up and initiate timing immediately and wait specified time for each parameter as indicated on the test strip container, then read each test zone only during the correct timeframes, comparing reagent pad colors to the manufacturer's color chart in good lighting
actions.resultName:
Color: Light yellow 
Glucose: 3+ (N: negative) 
Ketones: 1+ (N: negative) 
Interpretation: Glucosuria and ketonuria support uncontrolled hyperglycemia with developing ketosis.

communicationCriteria.title: Demonstrate empathy
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student demonstrated empathy. Look for acknowledging feelings, validating concerns, expressing care, and using reassuring language, not just clinical task completion. Return PASS only if there are clear empathic statements, FAIL if the encounter is purely transactional.

communicationCriteria.title: Use patient-centered communication strategies
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate patient-centered communication: open-ended questions, allowing the patient to elaborate, summarizing back, checking understanding, avoiding interruptions, and including the patient in decision-making. Return PASS if multiple patient-centered strategies are visible.

communicationCriteria.title: Establish rapport
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student established rapport with the patient at the start of the encounter. Did the student introduce themselves by name, confirm patient identity (name + DOB), use a warm tone, and orient the patient to what would happen? Return PASS only if most of these are present.

communicationCriteria.title: Use clear non-biased and non-stigmatizing language
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student uses clear non-biased and non-stigmatizing language when speaking with the patient and providing explanations of the plan of care or potential disease processes. Return PASS only if the student avoids use of any biased or stigmatizing language.

communicationCriteria.title: Demonstrate professional communication with a provider

aiPatientData.specialPatientInfo:
I usually describe what I’m feeling by saying I’m really thirsty all the time and going to the bathroom constantly. I’ll say I feel worn out and have trouble focusing in class. If you ask when this started, I’ll explain it’s been building over about a month and getting worse recently. 

 

If you ask about how often I’m peeing, I’ll say it’s a lot during the day and several times at night. If you ask about my appetite, I’ll say it’s about the same or sometimes even more, even though I’m losing weight. 

 

If you ask about drinks, I’ll admit I’ve been drinking a lot more sugary drinks because I feel so thirsty. If you ask about family history, I’ll mention my mom and grandmother having diabetes. 

 

When things are explained clearly, I understand and can repeat back that my blood sugar is high, that my body is making ketones, and that I need to go to the hospital to be treated safely. I might feel scared and worried about cost, but I’ll agree to the plan if it’s explained in a supportive way.

studentBriefing.purpose: The purpose of this simulation is to give you the opportunity to practice completing a focused assessment, obtaining and interpreting point‑of‑care glucose findings, and recognizing early signs of hyperglycemia and possible diabetic ketoacidosis in an adult patient. Working independently as the primary nurse, you will gather relevant history, complete appropriate nursing assessments, obtain a point-of-care blood glucose value, prepare to communicate concerns using SBAR, and provide clear, patient‑centered education and support. This experience is designed to strengthen your clinical judgment, safety awareness, and therapeutic communication skills when caring for an adult experiencing a potential metabolic emergency.

sbar.situation: The date and time of this simulated clinical encounter is: August 8th at 11:15. You are the primary nurse in the urgent care clinic today. Your patient is Emily Parker, a 21‑year‑old woman who checked in a short time ago reporting increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and an unintentional weight loss over the past several weeks. She states her symptoms have been getting worse recently.
sbar.background: Emily has no significant past medical history and takes only over‑the‑counter allergy medication, a combined oral contraceptive, and occasional ibuprofen. She denies recent illness, vomiting, or fever. She does not have an established primary care provider and has not previously been evaluated for these symptoms.
sbar.assessment:
At triage, she appeared tired but was alert and cooperative. Her initial vital signs were: 

HR: 104 bpm 
BP: 108/68 mmHg 
RR: 20/min 
Temp: 37.3°C (99.1°F) 
SpO₂: 98% on room air 

She is drinking water frequently in the waiting area and reports needing to use the restroom many times today.
sbar.recommendation: Please welcome Emily to the exam room, introduce yourself, and begin a focused history and assessment based on her presenting symptoms. Follow established orders and protocols for urgent care evaluation, including determining whether point‑of‑care testing is appropriate to obtain. Prepare to notify the provider of any concerning findings.
